name: Tower Bridge to Hyde Park
blurb: Along the Thames, past Westminster, and out to the park.

texts: Tower Bridge opened in 1894. Its roadway still lifts for tall ships, around eight hundred times a year.
Tower Bridge is often mistaken for London Bridge, which is the plainer one just upstream.
The climax of the 2009 Sherlock Holmes film is set high on Tower Bridge, while it is still being built.
For the 2012 Olympics, a giant set of Olympic rings hung from Tower Bridge's high walkway.
The London Marathon crosses Tower Bridge at about the halfway mark, one of the loudest spots on the course.
The Victoria Embankment was built in the 1860s over a new main sewer, on land reclaimed from the Thames.
Cleopatra's Needle, on the Embankment, is an Egyptian obelisk about three and a half thousand years old.
Every New Year's Eve, fireworks pour off the London Eye, just across the river from here.
In 2025 a new super sewer opened deep under the Thames, twenty-five kilometres long, to keep the river clean.
Big Ben is the bell, not the tower. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
For the film 28 Days Later, Westminster Bridge was emptied for a few minutes at dawn, so the city looked deserted.
For the Bond film Spectre, in 2015, Westminster Bridge was closed over several weekends to film a helicopter crash-landing on it.
The great clock is fine-tuned with old pennies. Each penny added to the pendulum makes it gain two fifths of a second a day.
Norway has sent a Christmas tree to Trafalgar Square every year since 1947, as thanks for help in the Second World War.
The fourth plinth in Trafalgar Square stands empty of a statue. Instead it shows a new piece of modern art every couple of years.
The statue at Piccadilly Circus is usually called Eros, but it was meant to be his brother, Anteros.
Piccadilly is named after piccadills, stiff lace collars made by a tailor who lived nearby.
In 28 Days Later, the hero wanders an empty Piccadilly Circus, beneath the statue of Eros.
The curved screen at Piccadilly Circus, put up in 2017, has around eleven million pixels, one of the largest of its kind in Europe.
Wellington Arch once carried an enormous statue of the Duke on horseback. It was moved away in the 1880s.
Wellington Arch once housed a tiny police station.
Marble Arch was designed as a gateway to Buckingham Palace, and moved here in 1851.
Near Marble Arch stood the Tyburn gallows, used for executions for about six hundred years.
By tradition, only senior royals and one troop of the King's artillery may pass through Marble Arch.
